The founder's numbers are pinned to the launch era (the founder's gap-11 rule): the YC company page as captured on

## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why5: My pick, people I know by name each with their own link, is kept exactly as I chose it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title with '4 beliefs: 4 holding' beside it, and each card carries its count against its bar, so I know it held and why.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on the stage page, only per-card count lines; most read at once, but Importance repeats '6 of 7 put it in their two' twice and Frequency packs a median, a count and a bar into one line, so I needed a second look.
screens.why_b3: The four dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, word for word, including Importance and Current solution.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next, such as moving on to whether directors will pay the €3,000 pilot; I only get the verdict and the rule that it is the worst card.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every line, but nothing says seven agents is a small sample, and four of four 'Holding up' reads firmer than seven people can carry.
screens.instead: Holding up on 7 reservation agents, a small sample: all four problem beliefs cleared their bars (Importance 6 of 7, Current solution 6 of 7), so the problem is real enough to test next whether revenue directors will pay for the €3,000 pilot.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I can see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip plainly counts yes answers, out of 7 people, with my bar marked at 6, and all three are clear on first look.
screens.why_b3: My belief was about booking calls that go unanswered, the 5% we miss after hours, at peak and on holidays, but this card tests whether a booking call came in on the shift at all, which is the circumstance every reservation agent is in and not my problem.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' tells me my problem is widespread, when all it shows is that agents get calls, so the next step it implies is wrong and I learn nothing about missed calls.
screens.why_b5: The card says my belief is 'Holding up' on a gate no working reservation agent could answer No to, so a 7-of-7 that could never have failed is presented as support for the missed-call problem, a claim the data cannot carry, even though the small n is flagged.
screens.instead: Ask 'In the last 7 days, did a booking call on your shift go unanswered?' so an agent who answered every call can say No, then tell me how many of the 7 actually missed one against my bar of 6.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits beside the deciding number, 6 of 7 inside my 5 to 7 days against a bar of 5 of 7, with the median of 6 days.
screens.why_b2: The count over 7 people and the bar at 5 of 7 are plain, but the legend's 'what you said · at what you said' needs a second look, and a 0 tick sits on a chart whose item had no 0.
screens.why_b3: The card is Frequency as I checked it, but the belief counts days a booking call came in, not days one rang out unanswered, which is my problem, so it is recognisable but drifted.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' points onward but says nothing about what calls every day means for missed-call cover on my shifts.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and 'a lean, not a call' is said, but 6 of 7 having a call come in reads as the problem being frequent when nobody was asked how often a call went unanswered, and 'the most recent time it happened' muddles a count-of-days question.
screens.instead: Count the days a booking call rang out unanswered on the agent's shift, drop 'the most recent time it happened', and say what 6 of 7 means for after-hours and peak cover.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, though the count is printed twice in a row, which reads like a glitch.
screens.why_b2: The caption says it plainly: 7 people, two picks each, 14 picks. My row's 6 stands out against the 2s, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against with the marker at 5.
screens.why_b3: The title is Importance and the belief line is the one I checked word for word, with my own item, Calling back missed booking calls, marked as the problem I named.
screens.why_b4: The So line only explains that two picks means top two, not first, and 'a lean, not a call' is a caveat; nothing says what to do with this for Codyco, such as leading with missed calls or what Chiara's call-center-after-six answer means for groups that already cover nights.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', the top-two-not-first limit is spelled out, and the one person against is shown with their reason.
screens.instead: Holding up among 7, a lean: missed booking calls are in nearly everyone's top two, so lead with them; but Chiara's group, whose call center covers after six, put emails and group requests first, so ask more groups with after-hours cover before counting on them. Show 6 of 7 once.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding numbers, 6 of 7 said today's way falls short against a bar of 5 of 7, and the chart, strip and list all agree on the 6 for and 1 against.
screens.why_b2: Each of the five rungs carries its count with the line drawn under 'A few rang out, all called back that day', and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5 of 7, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension name and the belief line are word for word the ones I checked, clumsy 'by the central reservations office or call center' phrasing and all, and the bar names my rung exactly.
screens.why_b4: The So line breaks down where the 6 fell short, but 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' is generic: it never says the gap is calls ringing out and not being called back, which is exactly what my AI answering would close, or what to test next.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 7 counted) and the screen says outright 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than the seven can carry.
screens.instead: For 6 of 7, calls rang out and were called back late or never (4 of them lost most or all of them); that is the gap an AI answering rung-out calls closes, so next test whether directors would forward those calls to it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict and its number sit together: "Importance held, 6 of 7", and the status line gives the bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b3: The line is named Importance and carries my belief word for word: calling back missed booking calls is one of the two things agents would most like made easier.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what this means for Codyco, for example that groups whose call center already covers after six are a weaker fit, or whether group emails and rate parity sit next to the phone problem.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and the single dissenter are plain, but Current solution gets no box and no note, unlike Prevalence and Frequency, so the one agent whose way does not fall short is silently missing.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's quote adds something I did not type: where a call center already takes the phones after six, the pain moves to group requests and emails that arrive with no rates, and keeping rates right across channels.

screens.why1: As the first screen it obviously checks whether I am the right person, someone taking booking calls for a hotel group's central reservations in Germany.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call centre are everyday words in my job in Munich, so I can answer at once.
screens.why3: I know exactly where I work and that our group runs a central reservations office, because I sit in it.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and a screener gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It only describes the kind of workplace and says nothing about any product or plan, so nothing leaks to me.
screens.why6: The question is short and easy to hear, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is stiff for a yes-or-no where 'Yes or no.' would do.
screens.instead: Do you work at a hotel group in Germany with a central reservations office or call centre? Yes or no.

screens.why1: A recent-time question fits here, but asking a reservation agent whether a booking call came in on her shift feels almost silly, since the screener already said this is my job.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether calls came in on my shifts last week, because they come in all day, every day.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product, plan or their own terms reaches me; it is just my work in my words.
screens.why6: One short question with the window up front, then 'Yes or no', so it is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks the circumstance, a call coming in, not the problem the founder counted, a call that was not answered or not turned into a booking; every agent says Yes, No has no one, and the share can never be refuted.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call on your shift go unanswered? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, calls came in on my shift, asking on how many days is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Booking call, shift, days: these are the words I use every day in the reservations office, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly which days I worked this week, and every one of them had booking calls, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 7, no overlap, no missing answer, and I can't recall sits apart as the only escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of anyone's product or plan reaches me; it is just a question about calls on my shift.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold and answer by phone.
screens.why7: The measure, shape and escape are right, but a booking call coming in is not the problem; in a central office every shift has calls, so my answer is just how many days I worked, and these options cannot speak for or against how often callers go unanswered.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many days did booking calls wait in the queue with no free agent on your shift? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 7 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After asking about booking calls on my shifts, asking which part of my shift I'd most like made easier is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Every option is in words we use in the office (rates, channels, group requests, call-backs), so I'd answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I work in the central reservations office, not at a hotel desk, so 'guests' requests at the desk' and the check-in and check-out rush are front-desk work I don't do and would have to skip or guess at.
screens.why4: The thing that actually hurts on a trade-fair Saturday, getting to every booking call before it rings out, is missing, and two of the five rows belong to the front desk, not to me.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the company's own terms reaches me; it reads like a plain question about my shift.
screens.why6: One short question and five short parallel options with one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The founder's own difficulty, answering every booking call before it rings out, is not among the options ('Calling back missed booking calls' is a look-alike chore after the fact), so nothing can count for the belief and it can only be refuted; two rows are also another setting's work.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Answering every booking call before it rings out; Calling back missed booking calls; Answering booking emails and group requests; Keeping rates right on every channel; or None of these.

screens.why1: After asking which part of the shift I'd most like made easier, asking how getting calls answered went last time follows naturally.
screens.why2: The stem pastes in 'central reservations office or call center', an either-or label I would never say about my own desk, and I had to read it twice to see it means us.
screens.why3: I know how my shift went for rung-out calls, but 'your last call' is one call, while the options are about many calls, so I would have to guess what it means.
screens.why4: The five options are distinct and in our words (rang out, called back), but they describe a shift, not the single last call the stem asks about, and 'Someone else did it' is a stretch for an agent on the desk.
screens.why5: The founder's segment label 'central reservations office or call center' came through word for word into the question, where I would just say 'the desk' or 'reservations'.
screens.why6: The stem is a mouthful when heard, with the long office-or-call-center clause, though the five options say well as a list.
screens.why7: It is one measure (whether rung-out calls got answered and when), with five rungs from working to failing outright and the one escape, so the belief can be tested both ways; but the stem asks about one call while the rungs grade a whole shift, which bends the rule that each option answers the exact question on that one occasion.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift on the reservations desk. How did getting the booking calls answered go? (same five options, then: Someone else did it)
